Lord sent me--</hi>a valid justification against any laws alleged against him.<div eID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against ... against--</hi>rather, "concerning." Jeremiah purposely avoids saying, "against," which would needlessly irritate. They had used the same Hebrew word (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">Jr 26:11</reference>), which ought to be translated "concerning," though they meant it in the unfavorable sense. Jeremiah takes up their word in a better sense, implying that there is still room for repentance: that his prophecies aim at the real good of the city; for or concerning this house ... city [Grotius]. <div eID="gen18127" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10163"/><div sID="gen18131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10163"/><hi type="bold">16. princes ... all the people--</hi>The fickle people, as they were previously influenced by the priests to clamor for his death (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.8">Jr 26:8</reference>), so now under the princes' influence require that he shall not be put to death. Compare as to Jesus, Jeremiah's antitype, the hosannas of the multitude a few days before the same people, persuaded by the priests as in this case, cried, Away with Him, crucify Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.11.27">Mt 21:1-11; 27</reference>:20-25). The priests, through envy of his holy zeal, were more his enemies than the princes, whose office was more secular than religious. A prophet could not legally be put to death unless he prophesied in the name of other gods (therefore, they say, "in the name of the Lord"), or after his prophecy had failed in its accomplishment. Meanwhile, if he foretold calamity, he might be imprisoned. Compare Micaiah's case (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.28">1Ki 22:1-28</reference>). <div eID="gen18131" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10167"/><div sID="gen18141" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10167"/>20. As the flight and capture of Urijah must have occupied some time, "the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim" (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.1">Jr 26:1</reference>) must not mean the very beginning, but the second or third year of his eleven years' reign.<div eID="gen18141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And ... also--</hi>perhaps connected with <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jr 26:24</reference>, as the comment of the writer, not the continuation of the speech of the elders: "And although also a man that prophesied ... Urijah ... (proving how great was the danger in which Jeremiah stood, and how wonderful the providence of God in preserving him), nevertheless the hand of Ahikam," &c. [Glassius]. The context, however, implies rather that the words are the continuation of the previous speech of the elders. They adduce another instance besides that of Micah, though of a different kind, namely, that of Urijah: he suffered for his prophecies, but they imply, though they do not venture to express it, that thereby sin has been added to sin, and that it has done no good to Jehoiakim, for that the notorious condition of the state at this time shows that a heavier vengeance is impending if they persevere in such acts of violence [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18142" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10168"/><div sID="gen18143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10168"/><hi type="bold">22. Jehoiakim sent ... into Egypt--</hi>He had been put on the throne by Pharaoh of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:34</reference>). This explains the readiness with which he got the Egyptians to give up Urijah to him, when that prophet had sought an asylum in Egypt. Urijah was faithful in delivering his message, but faulty in leaving his work, so God permitted him to lose his life, while Jeremiah was protected in danger. The path of duty is often the path of safety. <div eID="gen18143" type="x-p"/>

Ahikam--</hi>son of Shaphan the scribe, or royal secretary. He was one of those whom King Josiah, when struck by the words of the book of the law, sent to inquire of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.12">2Ki 22:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.14">14</reference>). Hence his interference here in behalf of Jeremiah is what we should expect from his past association with that good king. His son, Gedaliah, followed in his father's steps, so that he was chosen by the Babylonians as the one to whom they committed Jeremiah for safety after taking Jerusalem, and on whose loyalty they could depend in setting him over the remnant of the people in Judea (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.14">Jr 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22">2Ki 25:22</reference>).<div eID="gen18145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people to put him to death--</hi>Princes often, when they want to destroy a good man, prefer it to be done by a popular tumult rather than by their own order, so as to reap the fruit of the crime without odium to themselves (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.20">Mt 27:20</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.26"/>
